title: Round Hill is suing Suno and Anthropic for up to $1B apiece. It isn’t looking to settle.

reading.body:
The failure here is one of training data acquisition and output reproduction. Suno admitted to training on what it described as essentially all music files on the internet, and reporting based on a hack identified YouTube, Deezer, and Genius among the scraped sources. The outputs the system produced were not merely similar in style to existing recordings, they reproduced melodies and sonic characteristics closely enough that specific prompts reliably generated material mimicking specific artists and songs. That is a system producing outputs that carry the content of its training data rather than generating genuinely novel work.

The failure was embedded at the data-collection stage, before any user interaction. A licensing or rights-clearance review at that stage would have been the point at which it could have been caught. No such review is reported to have occurred. The system was then deployed publicly, meaning any user with a targeted prompt could extract material that closely matched copyrighted recordings.

What is not established is that any of the allegations of intentional theft constitute a legal finding of willful infringement. A German court ruled against Suno in GEMA's case, some plaintiffs reached settlements, and other lawsuits remain active, but allegations made in complaints and class actions are not verdicts, and the terms of settlements do not constitute admissions of liability unless explicitly stated.

summary:
Major record labels including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, Warner Music, Capitol Records, and Atlantic Records have filed lawsuits against AI music generators Udio and Suno. The labels accuse both companies of illegally scraping thousands of copyrighted songs without permission to train their AI models and then directly reproducing sections of famous recordings in their generated music. The record labels submitted a lengthy list of scraped works spanning artists like The Beatles, Michael Jackson, Frank Sinatra, Bruce Springsteen, and many others.

As evidence, the record labels demonstrated they could repeatedly recreate famous songs by entering specific prompts into the AI generators. For example, prompting "1954 rock and roll billy haley comets" produced outputs mimicking Bill Haley's style and melody, while a Mariah Carey prompt generated a near-identical clone of "All I Want for Christmas Is You." The record labels claim the companies have refused to disclose their training data and assert that such copyright infringement is fair use. Two separate lawsuits were filed, one in New York against Udio and one in Massachusetts against Suno, setting up a significant court battle over generative AI's use of copyrighted material.
